title: Loops
hook: `for`, `while`, and `do` are index or condition loops. `foreach` walks a sequence through `GetEnumerator` — the shape you want for CSV rows and SQS batches.

sections.heading: Walking sequences
sections.prose: `while (cond) { }` tests first. `do { } while (cond);` tests after at least one body. `for (init; cond; iter)` is the index form — use it when you have an array and a known bound, not as a default. `foreach (var row in rows)` is the idiomatic walk: it works on arrays, `List<T>`, and anything enumerable. You cannot assign to the iteration variable to mutate the collection slot (for most collections). Do not `foreach` and `Add` to the same `List` — the enumerator throws. High-concurrency attempt submit is not solved by a tighter loop; that is threading later. Here: pick `foreach` for a batch, `for` for index math.

snippets.label: foreach CSV rows versus indexed for
snippets.explanation: foreach is the default for a sequence. Use for when the index is part of the business rule (header row, window of 199–999).

interviewTakeaways: `foreach` is “walk a sequence,” not a special array syntax.
`do-while` always runs once; `while` may run zero times.
Mutating a list during `foreach` throws; build a new list or use `for` backwards when deleting.
commonPitfalls: Using `for` with `Count` on a LinkedList-like structure by habit — foreach (or LINQ later) is clearer.
Off-by-one when mixing 0-based indexes with CSV line numbers.

jsTsCorrelations.note: C# `foreach` is closest to `for...of`. `for...in` enumerates keys; there is no C# equivalent you should reach for on lists.
